Of 117 technology x stage cells and electro-industrial nodes assessed for the pair (not counting 25 cells whose products are read node by node), 25 show an active complementarity (a supplier meeting the other's need, a shared chokepoint, a capacity-constrained trusted supplier or a chain specialisation), 4 direct competition and 65 no strategic case. The relationship is not one of general similarity: most of the electro-industrial base needs no bilateral intervention.

AIB strategic roles: US Demand & Market Anchor (primary), Coordination / Bridge Hub (primary), Capital & Investment Anchor (primary), Scale Manufacturing & Integration Platform (secondary), Specialized Technology & Manufacturing Anchor (secondary); Japan Capital & Investment Anchor (primary), Specialized Technology & Manufacturing Anchor (primary), Scale Manufacturing & Integration Platform (primary), Coordination / Bridge Hub (secondary).

Japan supplies accumulator parts & separators, rare-earth permanent magnets, piezo-electric quartz, battery materials (foil, electrolyte) where the US is short; the US supplies polysilicon †, wind turbine generating sets †, refrigerants, sensors & controller parts where Japan is short; the two share exposure to coercive suppliers in rare-earth oxides & compounds, natural graphite, where neither can supply the other and the answer is joint demand, finance and third-country capacity; and they specialise at different steps of the same chains in wafers †, battery recycling feed, AC generators †.

From the AIB roles, the US brings demand and offtake, coordination across allied chains, capital; Japan brings capital, specialised technology and manufacturing, scale manufacturing. Public finance runs through DOE LPO, DoW OSC, DFC, EXIM on the US side and JBIC, NEXI, JOGMEC on the Japan side. The trade is market access and demand certainty for trusted capacity.

Quad leaders committed to identify and address gaps in manufacturing capacity for clean-energy technologies, focusing on solar PV, hydrogen electrolysers and EV batteries. They adopted joint principles for clean-energy supply chains and planned a public-private Quad Clean Energy Supply Chain Conference.

Australia was to open applications in Nov 2024 for the AUD 50m (about US$34m at Sep 2024 rates) programme supporting solar-panel, electrolyser and battery supply-chain projects in the Indo-Pacific. India committed US$2m to solar projects in Fiji, Comoros, Madagascar and Seychelles, and Japan US$122m to renewable projects. Awards and 2025-26 activity are not stated.

A joint statement in New York on 23 Sep 2024 set up a network of MSP export-credit agencies, development-finance institutions and state-backed funds. Its purpose is to share information, coordinate and co-finance critical-minerals projects. Named members include DFC, Export Development Canada, JICA, JBIC, KEXIM and Export Finance Norway among others.

Both sides in 2024 said the 2022-launched Economic 2+2 works as an effective economic-security framework and agreed to hold it periodically; no 2026 meeting found (Feb 2026 Rubio-Motegi and Ichikawa-Rubio contacts only).

G7 leaders adopted the plan at Kananaskis on 17 Jun 2025, under Canada's presidency. It tasks ministers with a roadmap for standards-based markets with traceability by year-end, calls on export credit agencies, DFIs and MDBs to scale up mining finance, and targets processing, recycling and substitution R&D. Australia, India and Korea later endorsed it.
Senior officials meeting in New York agreed to enhance dialogue on critical minerals and cooperation in Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa through the trilateral Early Warning System.

Announced in Toronto on 31 Oct 2025, this is the first round of the Production Alliance under the June 2025 G7 Critical Minerals Action Plan. Its 26 investments, partnerships and measures with France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Norway, the US, Australia and Ukraine aim to unlock C$6.4bn (about US$4.6bn at 0.71 USD/CAD) of graphite, rare-earth and scandium projects. They include Government of Canada offtakes with Nouveau Monde Graphite and Rio Tinto (scandium) and up to C$20.2m for joint R&D. Canada also released a roadmap for standards-based critical-minerals markets.

Adopted in Toronto on 31 Oct 2025 as an early action under the Action Plan, it aims to reduce and eventually eliminate dependence on supply chains dominated by non-market practices. It prioritises interoperable traceability systems aligned with the UN Transparency Protocol and lists price floors, procurement, tax and trade measures as tools members may use, with no deadlines.

Carney launched the Alliance at Kananaskis to use strategic investments and offtakes to bring critical-mineral projects into production for defence and advanced technology. At the 30-31 Oct 2025 Toronto ministerial, ministers agreed their critical-minerals envoys would advance the work, and Canada announced investments including offtakes with two Canadian projects. Member list, deal count, values and the US role are not stated in either source.
The US-hosted ministerial in Feb 2026 was attended by Japan and Korea among others, and Korea was reported to chair the FORGE critical-minerals forum through June 2026.

Korea chaired the Minerals Security Partnership until June 2026; a February 2026 report says its 17 members carried into the successor FORGE; Korean public lenders joined the MSP Finance Network; no signed US-Korea critical-minerals MOU was found.

At the 19 Feb 2026 Ministerial, IEA ministers endorsed an expanded phase of the Critical Minerals Security Programme, which was established in 2022. The expansion covers: support for members that set up or expand stockpiles; rapid market assessments and coordinated responses during supply disruptions; regular table-top exercises (a rare-earth exercise was held in Nov 2025); a wider information dashboard; a new Technology Collaboration Programme on recycling and substitution. The release gives no budget.
Quad foreign ministers adopted a framework to mobilise up to $20bn for secure critical-mineral supply chains; a separate July 2025 Quad initiative is mentioned only in passing and not sourced.
Launched July 2025 and framework adopted May 2026 to mobilise up to US$20bn of public and private support for mining, processing and recycling; no project list.

On 7 Oct 2026 the trade ministers of Argentina, Australia, Canada, the EU, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, Korea, Mexico, Poland, Turkiye, the UK and the US signed a statement committing to new sectoral platforms on structural excess capacity. The platforms start with autos and EVs, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors and solar panels, and officials are to meet at technical level before December 2026 to draft terms of reference and share data.

USTR is negotiating a binding plurilateral ATCM. Japan, Mexico and the EU are the first partners, building on action plans of 4 Feb, 19 Mar and 24 Apr 2026, and the design envisages phased-in, mineral-specific, border-adjusted price floors with common standards. As of 28 Sep 2026 no text was public, a reported initial scope of 5-10 minerals was unconfirmed and US implementing legislation would be needed. G7 trade ministers endorsed plurilateral agreements on 5-6 May 2026, and a Feb 2026 USTR comment request drew about 2,500 comments.

† Non-oriented electrical steel (NGO): Motor and generator laminations, so it sits with the drives chain, as GOES sits with transformers in SC-GRID. The data agree: NGO and GOES each form a workstream of their own. Alternative: one electrical-steel step in either compact, on the grounds that the same mills make both grades; rejected because the binding downstream bottlenecks (motor laminations, transformer cores) differ, and GOES is made by far fewer mills.

† AC generators: Same HS heading family (8501) and the same manufacturers as motors, and the same magnet and NGO inputs. Most of the value is large generators for hydro, thermal and nuclear plants, which take them as inputs from this compact. Alternative: SC-WIND, rejected because wind generating sets are traded complete (850231).
† Synthetic graphite (anode-grade): Anode material. The same graphitisation capacity also makes arc-furnace electrodes (SC-INDUSTRY).
† Manganese dioxide (EMD): Mostly for primary (alkaline) cells, partly an LMO cathode precursor; kept with the refined battery chemicals.

† Integrated circuits: Logic, memory and analog chips share wafers, fab equipment and gallium/germanium with power devices, so chips and power electronics are one compact. ICs are about 70% of its allied demand, so demand-weighted SC-SEMIS figures mostly describe ICs. Alternative: a separate chips compact (materials, fab equipment, ICs, sensors) with power semiconductors, components and converters as a Power Electronics compact; rejected for now because it splits the fab chain and would take an eleventh compact unless electric vehicles went back into SC-BATTERIES.

† Static converters & inverters: HS 850440 is one heading for solar and storage inverters, EV chargers, motor drives, UPS, ICT power supplies and HVDC/FACTS converters. Placed with the power semiconductors and passives it is assembled from. Alternative: SC-GRID as 'Grid Equipment & Power Electronics' (the name the task suggested), rejected because grid converters are a minority of the heading and it would turn SC-GRID into all electrical equipment; or SC-SOLAR, rejected for the same reason (solar inverters are one use among many).

† Power electronics components: Film capacitors, inductors and reactors, and parts of converters and transformers (850490 is shared with transformers). Placed with the converters, as the dictionary does (Power electronics sector). Alternative: SC-GRID for the reactor and transformer-parts share.
† Automatic controllers: Industrial regulators and controllers built from chips and sensors; the loosest process link in SC-SEMIS. Alternative: SC-INDUSTRY, rejected because they serve every sector.
† Polysilicon: Solar-grade polysilicon dominates this code; electronic-grade polysilicon also feeds semiconductor wafers.

† Wafers: HS 381800 covers solar and semiconductor wafers alike, and the dictionary files it under Semiconductor materials. Japan becomes the largest supplier once China is removed, so semiconductor-grade wafers are a large share of the trade. Kept in SC-SOLAR because the task's solar case is polysilicon -> wafers -> cells -> modules, the model's physical constraint for this node is solar wafer capacity (GCIM), and the solar case needs the whole chain. Since the 2026-10-21 run the data cluster wafers with sensors on a Japan-led semiconductor base; that workstream is filed under SC-SEMIS by override while the node stays on the solar spine. Alternative: SC-SEMIS as the substrate of chips and power devices; revisit if the code is split by grade.

† Wind turbine generating sets: The wind turbine itself (850231), so it stays on the wind spine. Direct-drive turbines take magnets and generators from SC-MAGNETS; it forms a workstream of its own. Alternative: SC-MAGNETS as the end of a magnets-to-generators chain, rejected because the node is the whole turbine, not its generator.

† Wind towers: HS 730820 covers steel towers and lattice masts generally, including transmission towers and telecom masts, not only wind towers. Kept with wind, where the dictionary puts it. Alternative: SC-GRID for the transmission-tower share.

† Hydro turbine parts: Hydropower shares heavy rotating equipment, castings, forgings and several turbine makers with wind, and is too small (about $0.7bn of allied demand with hydro turbines) for a compact of its own. Alternative: a firm-power grouping with SC-NUCLEAR (shared heavy forgings), rejected because it would blur the nuclear fuel-cycle compact; leaving it unmapped is not possible because it forms a workstream of its own, and every workstream needs a compact.

† Uranium conversion & enrichment: Holds HS 284410 (natural uranium compounds), most of which is mined U3O8 concentrate, beside enriched and depleted uranium (284420, 284430); the step is labelled to say so. A reporting-code artefact, not a division of labour: Kazakhstan's and Canada's concentrate exports read as conversion here, while Australia reports its concentrate under ore (261210). The better fix is to move 284410 into the uranium-ore split of config/aib_taxonomy_dictionary.yml, which needs a rerun of scripts/31-32 (2026-10-21 review).

† Nuclear reactors & enrichment machinery: One node for reactors (840110, about $130m of world trade) and isotope-separation machinery (840120, about $70m). By value it is mostly reactors, so it stays at the end of the chain. Alternative: the conversion & enrichment step, which suits the centrifuge share (Germany and the Netherlands among the top exporters); revisit if the codes are split.

† Copper ores & concentrates: Copper and aluminium are cross-cutting (motors, battery foil, cables). They sit in SC-GRID, where cables, overhead lines, building wire and transformer windings take most conductor metal. With aluminium wire rod they are about 65% of SC-GRID's allied demand, all LOW INTERVENTION under Decoupling. Alternative: a separate base-metals compact (copper is a critical-mineral diplomacy topic in its own right), rejected for now because it is a single-metal chain with no BUILD node and would take an eleventh compact; or unmapped as cross-cutting, rejected because ore-to-rod is a real chain into cables and windings.

† Electricity meters: Grid-edge equipment procured by the same distribution utilities and filed under Grid by the dictionary (Digital grid sector); placed at the network-equipment step because meters are not made from cables or transformers, and its parts (extended) sit at the components step. Its process link to the rest of SC-GRID is weak: meters are electronics. Alternative: SC-SEMIS beside sensors and controllers, rejected because the buyers, standards and security concerns are the grid's.

† Electric & plug-in cars: Vehicles integrate three chains (cells, motors, inverters and chips), so they are an end-use compact of their own, as heat pumps and electric furnaces are, matching the dictionary's Electrified End Uses index. Alternative: the integration step of SC-BATTERIES (the first draft), rejected because cars alone (about $180bn) would be half of that compact's allied demand, and car exporters would then dominate its country roles and coverage. The compact's spine has one core step because its upstream sits in the other compacts.

† Solar thermal water heaters: Not photovoltaic: a building heat appliance made from collectors, absorbers and tanks, so it sits with heat pumps. Alternative: SC-SOLAR, where the dictionary's Solar sector puts it, rejected because it shares no input or process with the PV chain.
† Electrolysers: HS 854330 also covers electroplating apparatus.

† Graphite electrodes: Consumable of electric-arc furnaces, the green-steel chain of this compact. Made by graphitising needle coke, the same process step as synthetic anode graphite. Alternative: SC-BATTERIES beside synthetic graphite (shared graphitisation capacity), rejected because its buyers and bottleneck are steelmaking.

Where the findings are weak or counterintuitive
Joint bets resting on a node need inherited from its cell (a proxy): Rare-earth oxides & compounds; Piezo-electric quartz; Natural graphite; Polysilicon †; Wind turbine generating sets †.

Japan has no listed trade position (under 1% of world supply) at nodes where the US has material demand: solar cells, PV modules & generators, uranium/fuel extraction: aggregated low-coverage sub-sectors (spent fuel & nuclear scrap, uranium ores), uranium conversion & enrichment †, nuclear reactors & enrichment machinery †, lithium chemicals, PV cover glass, wind towers †, heat pumps & AC units, solar thermal water heaters †, electricity meters †, transformers, hydro turbine parts †, blade core wood (balsa), overhead conductors, aluminium wire rod, direct-reduced iron (DRI/HBI). Trade data miss capability that is owned abroad or sold at home, so these nodes cannot show complementarity even where corporate evidence suggests it.

Product-definition caveats (†): Non-oriented electrical steel (NGO): Motor and generator laminations, so it sits with the drives chain, as GOES sits with transformers in SC-GRID. The data agree: NGO and GOES each form a workstream of their own. Alternative: one electrical-steel step in either compact, on the grounds that the same mills make both grades; rejected because the binding downstream bottlenecks (motor laminations, transformer cores) differ, and GOES is made by far fewer mills; AC generators: Same HS heading family (8501) and the same manufacturers as motors, and the same magnet and NGO inputs. Most of the value is large generators for hydro, thermal and nuclear plants, which take them as inputs from this compact. Alternative: SC-WIND, rejected because wind generating sets are traded complete (850231); Synthetic graphite (anode-grade): Anode material. The same graphitisation capacity also makes arc-furnace electrodes (SC-INDUSTRY); Manganese dioxide (EMD): Mostly for primary (alkaline) cells, partly an LMO cathode precursor; kept with the refined battery chemicals; Integrated circuits: Logic, memory and analog chips share wafers, fab equipment and gallium/germanium with power devices, so chips and power electronics are one compact. ICs are about 70% of its allied demand, so demand-weighted SC-SEMIS figures mostly describe ICs. Alternative: a separate chips compact (materials, fab equipment, ICs, sensors) with power semiconductors, components and converters as a Power Electronics compact; rejected for now because it splits the fab chain and would take an eleventh compact unless electric vehicles went back into SC-BATTERIES; Static converters & inverters: HS 850440 is one heading for solar and storage inverters, EV chargers, motor drives, UPS, ICT power supplies and HVDC/FACTS converters. Placed with the power semiconductors and passives it is assembled from. Alternative: SC-GRID as 'Grid Equipment & Power Electronics' (the name the task suggested), rejected because grid converters are a minority of the heading and it would turn SC-GRID into all electrical equipment; or SC-SOLAR, rejected for the same reason (solar inverters are one use among many); Power electronics components: Film capacitors, inductors and reactors, and parts of converters and transformers (850490 is shared with transformers). Placed with the converters, as the dictionary does (Power electronics sector). Alternative: SC-GRID for the reactor and transformer-parts share; Automatic controllers: Industrial regulators and controllers built from chips and sensors; the loosest process link in SC-SEMIS. Alternative: SC-INDUSTRY, rejected because they serve every sector; Polysilicon: Solar-grade polysilicon dominates this code; electronic-grade polysilicon also feeds semiconductor wafers; Wafers: HS 381800 covers solar and semiconductor wafers alike, and the dictionary files it under Semiconductor materials. Japan becomes the largest supplier once China is removed, so semiconductor-grade wafers are a large share of the trade. Kept in SC-SOLAR because the task's solar case is polysilicon -> wafers -> cells -> modules, the model's physical constraint for this node is solar wafer capacity (GCIM), and the solar case needs the whole chain. Since the 2026-10-21 run the data cluster wafers with sensors on a Japan-led semiconductor base; that workstream is filed under SC-SEMIS by override while the node stays on the solar spine. Alternative: SC-SEMIS as the substrate of chips and power devices; revisit if the code is split by grade; Wind turbine generating sets: The wind turbine itself (850231), so it stays on the wind spine. Direct-drive turbines take magnets and generators from SC-MAGNETS; it forms a workstream of its own. Alternative: SC-MAGNETS as the end of a magnets-to-generators chain, rejected because the node is the whole turbine, not its generator; Wind towers: HS 730820 covers steel towers and lattice masts generally, including transmission towers and telecom masts, not only wind towers. Kept with wind, where the dictionary puts it. Alternative: SC-GRID for the transmission-tower share; Hydro turbine parts: Hydropower shares heavy rotating equipment, castings, forgings and several turbine makers with wind, and is too small (about $0.7bn of allied demand with hydro turbines) for a compact of its own. Alternative: a firm-power grouping with SC-NUCLEAR (shared heavy forgings), rejected because it would blur the nuclear fuel-cycle compact; leaving it unmapped is not possible because it forms a workstream of its own, and every workstream needs a compact; Uranium conversion & enrichment: Holds HS 284410 (natural uranium compounds), most of which is mined U3O8 concentrate, beside enriched and depleted uranium (284420, 284430); the step is labelled to say so. A reporting-code artefact, not a division of labour: Kazakhstan's and Canada's concentrate exports read as conversion here, while Australia reports its concentrate under ore (261210). The better fix is to move 284410 into the uranium-ore split of config/aib_taxonomy_dictionary.yml, which needs a rerun of scripts/31-32 (2026-10-21 review); Nuclear reactors & enrichment machinery: One node for reactors (840110, about $130m of world trade) and isotope-separation machinery (840120, about $70m). By value it is mostly reactors, so it stays at the end of the chain. Alternative: the conversion & enrichment step, which suits the centrifuge share (Germany and the Netherlands among the top exporters); revisit if the codes are split; Copper ores & concentrates: Copper and aluminium are cross-cutting (motors, battery foil, cables). They sit in SC-GRID, where cables, overhead lines, building wire and transformer windings take most conductor metal. With aluminium wire rod they are about 65% of SC-GRID's allied demand, all LOW INTERVENTION under Decoupling. Alternative: a separate base-metals compact (copper is a critical-mineral diplomacy topic in its own right), rejected for now because it is a single-metal chain with no BUILD node and would take an eleventh compact; or unmapped as cross-cutting, rejected because ore-to-rod is a real chain into cables and windings; Electricity meters: Grid-edge equipment procured by the same distribution utilities and filed under Grid by the dictionary (Digital grid sector); placed at the network-equipment step because meters are not made from cables or transformers, and its parts (extended) sit at the components step. Its process link to the rest of SC-GRID is weak: meters are electronics. Alternative: SC-SEMIS beside sensors and controllers, rejected because the buyers, standards and security concerns are the grid's; Electric & plug-in cars: Vehicles integrate three chains (cells, motors, inverters and chips), so they are an end-use compact of their own, as heat pumps and electric furnaces are, matching the dictionary's Electrified End Uses index. Alternative: the integration step of SC-BATTERIES (the first draft), rejected because cars alone (about $180bn) would be half of that compact's allied demand, and car exporters would then dominate its country roles and coverage. The compact's spine has one core step because its upstream sits in the other compacts; Solar thermal water heaters: Not photovoltaic: a building heat appliance made from collectors, absorbers and tanks, so it sits with heat pumps. Alternative: SC-SOLAR, where the dictionary's Solar sector puts it, rejected because it shares no input or process with the PV chain; Electrolysers: HS 854330 also covers electroplating apparatus; Graphite electrodes: Consumable of electric-arc furnaces, the green-steel chain of this compact. Made by graphitising needle coke, the same process step as synthetic anode graphite. Alternative: SC-BATTERIES beside synthetic graphite (shared graphitisation capacity), rejected because its buyers and bottleneck are steelmaking
Low-evidence units among the active states: none.

Trade data understate concentration at uranium conversion & enrichment †: enrichment is sold as a service under long-term contracts, so goods trade understates Russia's share of world enrichment capacity (roughly 40%), and the 2024 US ban on Russian low-enriched uranium imports makes trusted capacity the binding constraint.

Trade data understate concentration at gallium, germanium & indium: China's export controls since 2023 cut its recorded exports, so 2024 trade understates its share of primary gallium and germanium output (the large majority of world supply).

Fuel-trade lanes reach tier 1 (oil extraction; buyer: Japan): real energy-security lanes, but outside the electro-industrial compacts and with no market failure beyond the supply concentration the engine measures.
